subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: A source has a decay constant of 0.02 per second and 5.0 x 10^6 undecayed nuclei. Its activity is approximately:
Radioactive decay is described as random and spontaneous, meaning it:
options: always occurs at a fixed time
is unaffected by external conditions like temperature
can be predicted for individual nuclei
questions.explain: Decay is spontaneous (unaffected by external factors) and random (unpredictable for a single nucleus).

questions.q: Nuclear fusion of small nuclei releases energy because the product nucleus has:
questions.explain: Fusing light nuclei moves up the steep left side of the curve, increasing binding energy per nucleon.

questions.q: Experiments show nuclear radius R relates to nucleon number A by:
questions.explain: Nuclear radius scales as R = r0 A^(1/3), where r0 is about 1.2 fm.

questions.q: Which type of radiation is most strongly ionising?
questions.explain: Alpha particles are heavy and doubly charged, making them the most ionising.

questions.q: Alpha radiation is typically stopped by:
options: a few cm of air or paper
questions.explain: Alpha particles are absorbed by a sheet of paper or a few centimetres of air.

questions.q: In a magnetic field, alpha and beta-minus particles deflect:
questions.explain: They carry opposite charges (alpha positive, beta-minus negative) so deflect in opposite directions.

questions.q: The fact that R is proportional to A^(1/3) implies that nuclear density is:
questions.explain: Mass is proportional to A and volume to R^3 (i.e. A), so density is roughly constant across nuclei.

questions.q: On the N-Z stability graph, light stable nuclei lie:
options: close to the N = Z line
questions.explain: Light stable nuclei lie near N = Z; heavier ones need more neutrons (curve above the line).

questions.q: The greater the binding energy per nucleon, the:
questions.explain: Higher binding energy per nucleon indicates a more tightly bound, more stable nucleus.

questions.q: A chain reaction is sustained when each fission event causes on average:
questions.explain: A self-sustaining chain reaction requires at least one neutron per fission to trigger another.

questions.q: Which radiation is the most penetrating?
questions.explain: Gamma rays are highly penetrating, requiring thick lead or concrete to attenuate.

questions.q: Gamma radiation differs from alpha and beta in that it:
questions.explain: Gamma radiation is a high-energy photon (electromagnetic wave) with no mass or charge.

questions.q: The number of undecayed nuclei after time t is given by:
questions.explain: Radioactive decay follows an exponential law N = N0 e^(-lambda t).

questions.q: A nucleus above the stability line (neutron-rich) typically decays by:
questions.explain: Neutron-rich nuclei undergo beta-minus decay, converting a neutron to a proton.

questions.q: The nucleus with the highest binding energy per nucleon is around:
questions.explain: Iron-56 sits near the peak of the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve, the most stable region.

questions.q: The decay constant lambda represents the:
options: probability per unit time that a nucleus decays
questions.explain: Lambda is the probability of decay of a nucleus per unit time.

questions.q: In the equation E = mc^2, the c^2 emphasises that a small mass corresponds to:
questions.explain: Because c^2 is enormous, even a tiny mass defect releases a very large amount of energy.

questions.q: Which graph correctly describes how the activity of a sample changes with time?
questions.explain: Activity A = lambda N decreases exponentially because N decreases exponentially.

questions.q: The relationship between half-life T-half and decay constant lambda is:
questions.explain: Setting N = N0/2 in the decay law gives T-half = ln2/lambda.

questions.q: A mass defect of 1.0 u corresponds to a binding energy of approximately:
questions.explain: One atomic mass unit is equivalent to about 931.5 MeV of energy.

questions.q: A sample has a half-life of 8 days. What fraction remains after 24 days?
questions.explain: 24 days is three half-lives, so (1/2)^3 = 1/8 of the sample remains.

questions.q: Which is a typical product set of uranium-235 induced fission?
options: Two lighter daughter nuclei plus two or three neutrons
Two equal helium nuclei and no neutrons
questions.explain: U-235 fission produces two unequal daughter nuclei plus 2-3 neutrons and energy.

questions.q: In induced fission, the particle absorbed to make a heavy nucleus unstable is a:
questions.explain: A slow neutron is captured, making the nucleus unstable so it splits.

questions.q: The activity of a radioactive sample is given by:
questions.explain: Activity equals the decay constant multiplied by the number of undecayed nuclei, A = lambda N.

questions.q: Fusion in stars requires very high temperatures mainly to:
options: overcome the electrostatic repulsion between nuclei
questions.explain: High kinetic energy lets positively charged nuclei approach closely despite Coulomb repulsion.

questions.q: Mass defect is defined as the:
options: difference between the mass of the constituent nucleons and the nucleus
questions.explain: Mass defect is the difference between the total mass of separate nucleons and the assembled nucleus.

questions.q: Nuclear fission of a large nucleus releases energy because the products have:
questions.explain: The fragments lie nearer the peak of the curve with higher binding energy per nucleon, releasing energy.

questions.q: Binding energy is the energy:
options: required to separate a nucleus into its individual nucleons
questions.explain: Binding energy equals the work needed to completely separate a nucleus into free nucleons.

questions.q: The mass defect (delta m) and binding energy E are related by:
questions.explain: Einstein's mass-energy equivalence gives E = delta m c^2.
